# Language principles


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

BasedPL (BPL) keeps APL’s glyphs and its right-to-left evaluation. It
changes the notation where APL’s rules make code harder to read or to
write. Most of the changes follow from one decision, to write lists in
brackets. BasedPL stands for Based-array Programming Language, after the
array model it takes from BQN.

Many of the notation choices answer problems that Marshall Lochbaum,
BQN’s author, lists in his notes on [BQN’s
problems](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/problems.html) and
on [its first five
years](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/fiveyears.html).
[Syntax](syntax.qmd) and [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd) state the rules
without the reasons. [BPL, APL and BQN side by side](comparison.qmd)
shows the choices on real code.

## Lists are written in brackets

In APL, arrays written side by side form a list. `1 2 3`, `a b c` and
`(x+1) y` are all vectors. This is called stranding. It’s short, but it
gives a space a different job in different places. Between arrays, a
space separates the items of a list. Between functions it means nothing:
`+/÷≢` and `+ / ÷ ≢` are the same [train](terms.qmd#term-train). Between
an operator and an array, it can do either.

That last case causes real trouble. An operator takes the single value
to its right as its operand, after stranding has already joined that
value to its neighbours. In APL, the operand in `f⍤1 M` is `1 M`. You
have to write `f⍤1⊢M`, where
[`⊢`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/right-tack.html) is
there only to break the strand. BQN’s documentation gives the example
`a +˝∘×⎉1‿∞ b`, a matrix product. No rule decides well which of `1`,
[`∞`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/infinity.html) and
`b` should strand together. BQN marks its strands with `‿` instead.

In BPL, lists are written in brackets, `[a b c]`, as in Python and
JavaScript. Lochbaum notes that new BQN programmers “are always
expecting `[]` to be the list notation, and it’d let you copy-paste JSON
too”. You can still omit the brackets around a list of literals, as in
`1 2 3` and `"no" "yes"`. Inside brackets, names and literals mix
freely:

``` bpl
x←5
[1 x 3]
```

    1 5 3

Outside brackets, arrays side by side form a list too, whatever the
names hold. `+/x 3` is a two-item list whether `x` is a vector or a
matrix. Each [run](terms.qmd#term-run), a sequence of tokens with no
spaces between them, is one item of the list. In `a b+1` the items are
`a` and `b+1`. A bracket list is one run like any other:

``` bpl
a←1 ◇ b←2
a b+1
[1 2] 3
```

    1 3

    [[1 2] 3]

A bracket list is a vector, however many items it has. `[1]` is a
one-item vector, not a number:

``` bpl
ρ[1]
```

    [1]ₓ

Parentheses only group, as they do in maths. `(1 2)` is the same value
as `1 2`. To make a scalar, enclose with
[`⊂`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/left-shoe.html), as
in BQN. `⊂[1 2]` is a scalar, an array with no axes, holding a vector:

``` bpl
ρ⊂[1 2]
```

    ⍬ₓ

A function after
[`⊂`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/left-shoe.html) makes
a train instead, as in `⊂+`. The scalar holding
[`+`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/plus.html) is written
[`+ˢ`](scripts.ipynb#a-function-as-a-scalar).

Array notation extends brackets to higher ranks, as Dyalog’s does. Rows
separated by
[`◇`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/diamond.html), or
written on separate lines, become [major
cells](terms.qmd#term-major-cell):

``` bpl
[1 2
 3 4]
```

    1 2
    3 4

The result has one more axis than each row. When the rows are numbers,
which have no axes, the result is a vector. When the rows are one-item
vectors, the result is a column:

``` bpl
[1◇2]
[[1]◇[2]]
```

    1 2

    1
    2

`[a◇b]` is the Mix of `[a b]` when `a` and `b` have the same shape.

In parentheses, rows form a new level of nesting instead of a new axis.
Each row is one item of a vector, read as if written in brackets. The
rows can have different lengths:

``` bpl
≢¨(4◇4 5◇4 5 6)
```

    [1 2 3]ₓ

A row holding one string is still a vector of one item. `("ab"◇"cd")`
holds two one-item vectors, while `["ab" "cd"]` is the vector of two
strings:

``` bpl
≢¨("ab"◇"cd")
≢¨["ab" "cd"]
```

    [1 1]ₓ

    [2 2]ₓ

Items in brackets can be functions. `[+/ ÷ ≢]` holds three functions.
Without the spaces, `[+/÷≢]` holds one, the mean:

``` bpl
≢[+/ ÷ ≢]
≢[+/÷≢]
```

    3ₓ

    1ₓ

Writing a function expression in brackets is one way to make it a value.
In BQN this takes `⊑⟨Expr⟩` or a name, a problem Lochbaum lists as
“Converting a function expression to a subject is tricky”. The other way
is `fˢ`, a scalar holding the function `f`.

Items in a list are evaluated left to right, as statements are. BQN
chose the same order for its lists and strands. Here each item prints as
it’s evaluated, before the list itself is displayed:

``` bpl
[⎕←1 ⎕←2]
```

    1
    2

    1 2

## Spaces group

Outside brackets, literals separated by spaces form a strand, as in
`1 2 3`. Every other space separates runs. Each run is evaluated first,
as if it were in parentheses:

``` bpl
c←3 ◇ d←4
a+b×c+d
a+b × c+d
```

    15

    21

A space can separate a derived function from its argument: `+/⍤1 m`
applies `+/⍤1` to `m`. A run ending in a dyadic operator takes the next
run as its operand, as if no space came between them. A literal argument
after a space still joins the operand’s strand, as in `f⍤1 2 3`, whose
operand is `1 2 3`. The separator
[`⁝`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/tricolon.html)
(Alt-:) keeps tokens apart without ending the run. It separates names
that would merge and literals that would strand. All three of these sum
each row:

``` bpl
m←2 3ρι6ₓ
+/⍤1 m
+/⍤ 1 m
+/⍤1⁝2 3ρι6ₓ
```

    [3 12]ₓ

    [3 12]ₓ

    [3 12]ₓ

A space after an operator also lets a longer function be its operand
without parentheses. `⌊@ 10×` rounds down to one decimal place, with
`10×` as the operand of
[`@`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/at.html):

``` bpl
⌊@ 10× 1.24 3.57
```

    1.2 3.5

Lochbaum describes the problem that runs solve, under “Modifiers look
looser than trains without spaces”. In BQN’s `⋆∘-×˜`, the
[`-`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/minus.html) looks
closer to `⋆`, but it binds to `×˜`. Writing `⋆∘- ×˜` shows the
structure. He calls it “unfortunate that this is something the writer
must do rather than something the notation encourages”. In BPL the space
is part of the notation.

Under “Long trains are hard for humans to parse”, he notes that readers
lose track of a train’s structure after four to eight parts. Runs let
spaces show that structure. `⌊ +/÷≢` is the floor of the mean:

``` bpl
⌊ +/÷≢ 1 2 4
```

    2ₓ

Code that is fully spaced, or not spaced at all, groups as in APL. Only
mixed spacing changes the grouping. A reader used to APL reads `1+2 × 3`
as 7, but here it’s 9:

``` bpl
1+2 × 3
```

    9

A tool that normalises spaces would change a program’s meaning. Other
languages give spaces meaning too. K reads `a -1` differently from
`a - 1`. Nim tried an experimental mode in which the spaces around an
operator changed its precedence, and removed it in version 0.20.

## A run that ends in a function is a train

A run that ends in a function has no argument yet. It’s a function,
built as an APL train with one addition. A subject before a function
[binds](terms.qmd#term-bind) the one [part](terms.qmd#term-part) after
it, as `2` does in `2×`. Here `32+1.8×` converts Celsius to Fahrenheit:

``` bpl
f←32+1.8×
f100
```

    212

The rest follows APL’s train rules. A bound part such as `0.5×` forms an
[atop](terms.qmd#term-atop) with the train after it. In `0.5×⊢+÷`, that
atop gives the same result as Dyalog’s fork, whose left part is the
subject `0.5`. Binding covers the common case of fixing a left argument,
without
[`↣`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/right-tail-arrow.html).
K has the same idea, called projection, in which `2*` is a function.

`+/÷≢ nums` and `+/÷≢nums` differ only in the space before `nums`. The
first applies the train `+/÷≢`, the mean, to `nums`. The second is one
run ending in a subject, the expression `+/(÷(≢nums))`:

``` bpl
nums←1 2 3 6
+/÷≢ nums
+/÷≢nums
```

    3

    0ₓ

If both spellings meant the same, the space would mean nothing. In
everyday arithmetic, where the functions have arrays between them, as in
`32+1.8×`, the train gives the same result as the expression. The
readings differ only when a fork gets a function as its left part, as in
`0.5×⊢+÷`. APL has the same split, with nothing in the source to mark
it. Removing the argument from APL’s `0.5×⊢+÷ω` turns it into a fork
with a different meaning. In BPL the space shows which reading you get.

## Selection is a function

Index [`⌷`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/squad.html)
selects. `I⌷Y` takes one item of `I` for each leading axis of `Y`. In K,
`v 1` selects, because K treats a list as a function of its positions.
In BPL `v 1` is a strand, because subjects and functions stay apart. One
literal position can be written more briefly as a
[subscript](scripts.ipynb#subscripts), as in `v₁`:

``` bpl
v←10 20 30 40
1⌷v
v₁
```

    20

    20

Selecting with a number drops that axis from the result. Selecting with
an array of positions puts the array’s shape in place of the axis.
`[⊂1]⌷v` gives a scalar holding the item, `[[1]]⌷v` a one-item vector,
and `[[2 0]]⌷v` two items:

``` bpl
[⊂1]⌷v
[[1]]⌷v
[[2 0]]⌷v
```

    ⊂20

    [20]

    30 10

Dyalog has the same rule, but its `v[1]` looks like a one-item list and
gives a scalar. To get a one-item vector in Dyalog, write `v[,1]`.

Because Index takes its positions on the left, its right argument can be
any expression. With `sales` [keyed](keyed.ipynb) by city and month,
`"NY"⌷+/sales` selects New York’s total with no parentheses:

``` bpl
sales←["NY" "LA";"jan" "feb"]:[1 2◇3 4]
sales
"NY"⌷+/sales
```

       jan feb
    NY   1   2
    LA   3   4

    3

## Counting from 0

Positions and axes count from 0, as in BQN, J, K, Python and NumPy.
Negative positions count from the end.

- A Boolean is a valid position, as in `c⌷"no" "yes"`. With 1-origin,
  the position would be `1+c`.
- Positions run from `¯n` to `n-1` with no gap. With 1-origin, position
  0 is an error between position `1`, the first item, and position `¯1`,
  the last.
- `n|i` wraps a position round a vector of length `n`. `⌊i÷n` and `n|i`
  give the row and column of a flat position.
- The Python API returns positions from functions such as `grade` and
  `where`. Those positions must agree with Python and NumPy, which count
  from 0.

Here the comparison’s result is used as the position:

``` bpl
3>2 ⌷ "no" "yes"
```

    "yes"

To count from 1, use [Range](glyphs/right-arrow-from-bar.qmd): `↦10` is
the numbers 1 to 10. Code from APL books and libraries assumes 1-origin
and needs converting.

Two rules follow J and BQN where 0-origin left a choice. With a negative
length, [Iota](glyphs/iota.qmd) counts down, as J’s `i._3` does:

``` bpl
ι¯3
```

    2 1 0

Interval Index counts the boundaries at or below each value, as BQN’s
does. Below the first boundary the count is 0. If it returned a
boundary’s position instead, the position below the first boundary would
be `¯1`, which selects the last item:

``` bpl
1 3 5⍸0 3 9
```

    [0 2 3]ₓ

A negative position that a program computes also counts from the end.
With [dot brackets](glyphs/dot.qmd), as in `w.[i-1]`, the position for
`i=0` is `¯1`. `w.[i-1]` then gives the last item, as `w[i-1]` does in
Python. For a different result at the edge, wrap with `n|i-1` or clamp
with `0⌈(n-1)⌊i-1`:

``` bpl
w←10 20 30 40 ◇ i←ι4ₓ
w.[i-1ₓ]
w.[0⌈3⌊i-1ₓ]
```

    40 10 20 30

    10 10 20 30

## Based arrays

BPL uses BQN’s [based array
model](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/based.html). Numbers,
characters and functions are atoms. An array is a rectangular collection
of values. Atoms are not arrays. Enclosing always adds a layer: `⊂3` is
a rank-0 array holding 3, a different value from 3. Enclosing it again
gives depth 2:

``` bpl
⊂3 ≡ 3
≡⊂⊂3
```

    $f

    2ₓ

In APL’s nested array model, enclosing 3 gives 3 again. Under the based
model, every value has one representation, whether you pass it to a
function, return it, or store it in an array. `[+/ ÷ ≢]` is a list of
three functions. Lochbaum’s page on the model gives the longer argument.

## Under static kinds, number types don’t depend on values

Under [static kinds](numbers.qmd#static-kinds), a number’s type comes
from how the program writes or computes it, never from its value. If a
number’s type changed with its value, a program that works on one input
could behave differently on another. Static kinds are the setting for
performance work, such as training neural networks.
[Performance](performance.qmd) shows what they speed up. Dynamic kinds,
the default, are for convenient interactive analysis. Under dynamic
kinds, integers are exact and never wrap, and float comparisons are
tolerant. Under dynamic kinds, some results take their type from their
values: `√¯4` is complex, whereas `√4` is a float. Under either setting,
BPL doesn’t make a float exact because it happens to be whole: `2.0` is
a float, and so is `2.0+1`. To get exact integers, use `ₓ`.

## Functions act on major cells

BPL follows BQN’s leading-axis model. A function that works on a whole
array acts on its major cells, the cells along its first axis. The
last-axis glyphs `⌽ / \ ,` are the leading-axis functions applied at
rank 1. Their first-axis forms `⌽₀ ⌿ ⍀ ⍪` are the leading-axis functions
themselves. Every function therefore treats a matrix by the same rule.

Search follows that rule. `ι ∊ ~ ∪ ∩` compare the major cells of the
searched argument, which for a matrix are its rows. Here
[`~`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/tilde.html) removes
every row that is `1 2`, leaving a one-row matrix:

``` bpl
rows←[1 2
      3 4
      1 2]
rows~[1 2◇5 6]
ρrows~[1 2◇5 6]
```

    3 4

    [1 2]ₓ

The other argument is compared in cells of the same rank as those major
cells. A [unit](terms.qmd#term-unit) has no major cells to search. To
remove the spaces from a string, give
[`~`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/tilde.html) the
string `" "`. Giving it the character `' '`, a unit, raises a `RANK`
error:

``` bpl
"a b c"~" "
```

    "abc"

Partition splits along the first axis too, into blocks of major cells.
Here new blocks start at rows 0 and 2:

``` bpl
1 0 1⊂rows
```

    [[1 2◇3 4] [1 2◇]]

`⊂¹` applies Partition at rank 1, which partitions each row instead, and
`⊂₁` applies it along axis 1, which splits a matrix into blocks of
columns.

Encode and Decode put digits on the last axis, as J’s `#:` and `#.` do.
Encode turns each number of a vector into a row of digits. Decode turns
the rows back into numbers:

``` bpl
d←2 2 2⊤5 6
d
2⊥d
```

    1 0 1
    1 1 0

    5 6

At rank 0, the function gets each atom as itself and each array item
enclosed in a scalar. BQN’s `⎉0` encloses atoms as well. The depth of
each 0-cell shows the difference:

``` bpl
≡⁰ [1 [2 3]]
```

    [0 2]ₓ

As a result, `⊢⁰` returns its argument unchanged, even when the argument
is nested. At rank 0, a function receives each number as the atom that a
literal or selection gives, not enclosed in a scalar. Each
[`¨`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/diaeresis.html) gives
the function the items themselves.

## Names pair axes

Without names, arithmetic pairs axes by position, from the leading axis,
as [Agreement](evaluation.qmd#agreement-and-pervasion) describes. When
axes have names, they pair by name instead. Two axes with the same name
pair, whatever their positions. A named axis pairs with an unnamed axis
by position, and the result axis keeps the name. Two axes with different
names never pair. In arithmetic, axes with different names build a grid,
as an outer product does.

Pairing by position can pair the wrong axes. Here `r` has a row for each
item of a batch and a column for each output. `bias` has a value for
each output. By position, `bias` pairs with the rows instead. Because
the number of rows equals the length of `bias`, no error shows the
mistake:

``` bpl
r←2 2ρι4ₓ ◇ bias←[10 20]ₓ
r+bias
```

    [10 11
     22 23]ₓ

With names on both arrays, `bias` pairs with the output axis:

``` bpl
r←["b":2 "o":2]ρι4ₓ ◇ bias←["o":2]ρ[10 20]ₓ
r+bias
```

    [10 21
     12 23]ₓ

Selection also pairs axes by name, so a formula written with named
indices reads as [index notation](index-notation.qmd), with a name where
einsum has a letter. [`•index`](system/index.qmd) gives an index a fresh
hidden name, which can’t collide with the names on a caller’s data. An
index used twice pairs with itself, so `m.[i i]` is a diagonal:

``` bpl
m←[1 2 3◇4 5 6◇7 8 9] ◇ i←•index 3
m.[i i]
```

    1 5 9

No feature requires names. A function written for unnamed axes also runs
on arrays with named axes. If it gives different values on arrays with
named axes, the difference comes from how the names align the axes.
[Named axes](keyed.ipynb#named-axes) gives the full rules.

## Results rather than errors

A form that has a reasonable meaning gives a result, not an error. BPL
returns a result without error even when that result would be a bug in
some programs, if doing so gives useful behaviour or speed. Negative
positions are one case, as “Counting from 0” shows. Using
[`⌈`](glyphs/upstile.qmd) with NaN is another case. It gives NaN or the
other argument, whichever the processor’s fastest instruction gives. The
answer can differ between platforms.
